name: Failo

lead: "Failo" is community slang for a flaw or fail in someone's appearance, such as hair loss, a narrow palate or ears. Naming a failo is the first step to deciding whether to correct it or hide it.
The term is a vocabulary item, not a method, and no research addresses it.

paras: Users post photos or ask "is this a failo?", and others suggest fixes ranging from grooming and style changes to procedures. One thread shows a guide to improving a wide eye-spacing ratio without surgery.
Threads can encourage fixation on small details; this is community behaviour rather than a physical risk.

angle.text: The term frames a feature as something to address. Members then discuss grooming, style or procedure options.

lead: Failo is looksmaxxing slang for a flaw or fail in someone's appearance, a feature that is seen as pulling the overall look down. Naming a failo is the first step in the ascension routine: once a feature is identified, members discuss whether to correct it with grooming, styling, fitness or a procedure, or to work around it with a haircut, facial hair or clothing.[1][2][3][4]

Community glossaries describe a failo as the opposite of a halo (a lift in how a face is read); where a halo is a feature that lifts how the rest of a face or person is read, a failo is a feature that drags it down. The pairing parallels the halo effect and horn effect from social psychology, in which one trait colours impressions of a person overall.[5][6]

Threads on looksmax.org ask whether specific features count as failos, such as big calves, a narrow palate, ear shape, lips, a long philtrum or the midface, and others use the word for style choices, a haircut, or a wide eye-spacing ratio.[1][2][3][4][7][8][9][10] No published study has examined the term itself.

paras: Failo belongs to the vocabulary of looksmaxxing, an online practice of maximising physical attractiveness that emerged on forums in the 2010s and spread to TikTok and livestreams in the 2020s.[5][11] Related terms include mogging (outshining another person's appearance), halo, ascension, softmaxxing (non-invasive routines such as skincare, grooming and fitness) and hardmaxxing (more invasive methods).[5]

A failo is described as the counterpart to a halo. Members use "failo" for a single feature, as in "how much of a failo is a narrow palate", and for the effect of a feature on the whole, as in threads naming the midface or the long philtrum as the worst failo to have.[2][7][8]

The idea works as an audit. A member posts photos, asks "what's my biggest failo", and others point to features and propose a fix or a styling workaround.[12] Threads cover features across the body, from big calves to the palate and ears.[1][2][3] Another thread discusses lips as a possible failo.[10]

One thread presents a guide on "fixing" a wide eye-spacing ratio (ESR), a metric comparing the distance between the eyes to the width of one eye, which the author describes as typically considered ideal at about 1:1. The author argues for non-surgical alternatives to orbital box osteotomy, a rare and expensive operation, and uses a before-and-after photo of a user as the reference.[4]

Another thread lists lower-third jaw surgeries matched to a user's failo, and others rank a long philtrum or the midface as the worst failo to have.[13][7][8] Another thread blames a bad haircut for making someone's appearance worse, which shows the word also covers fixable style choices.[9]

The halo effect was named by psychologist Edward Thorndike, who in a 1920 paper found that officers' ratings of soldiers' separate qualities were correlated more strongly than expected.[6] In 1972 Dion, Berscheid and Walster showed participants photos of attractive, average and unattractive people and found that attractive people were assumed to have more desirable traits and happier lives.[6] The horn effect is the negative counterpart, in which one disliked trait colours the overall perception of a person.[6] Looksmaxxing slang uses "halo" and "failo" for the same asymmetry.

Failo threads on looksmax.org take the form of rating requests, rankings and arguments about whether a trait matters.[1][2][3][12] The word is also applied to fixable style choices such as a haircut.[9]

Mainstream coverage of looksmaxxing spread the broader vocabulary in 2025 and 2026. WIRED writer Miles Klee described terms such as looksmaxxing and mogging as moving from niche forums into everyday commentary, crediting streamer Braden Peters, known as Clavicular, for much of the recent spread.[11] Wikipedia notes that critics describe the practice as judgmental and associate it with body-image harm, while some commentators note potential benefits such as improved health habits.[5]
No studies found. Research on the halo and horn effects is described under Psychological background.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, failo is used both for individual features and for judgments about their effect on the whole look.[1][2][3] Members debate whether given features are important and whether they can be fixed.

claims.claim: Individual features can act as a failo that lowers the whole look.
A wide eye-spacing ratio can be improved without orbital surgery.
A strong halo can offset a failo.
Surgery is the fix for a structural failo.

timeline.event: Psychologist Frederick Wells identifies what later becomes known as the halo effect.[6]
Edward Thorndike publishes 'A Constant Error in Psychological Ratings', naming the halo effect.[6]
Dion, Berscheid and Walster publish photo-rating research on physical attractiveness and assumed traits.[6]
Looksmaxxing vocabulary develops on forums including Lookism.net.[5]
Failo threads appear regularly on looksmax.org, covering features such as the palate, ears and eye-spacing ratio.[1][2][3][4]
WIRED reports looksmaxxing slang entering mainstream commentary.[11]
